item.title: Antiferroelectric hafnia down to the 2D limit
item.dc:creator: Xin Li
Guodong Ren
Haidong Lu
Kartik Samanta
Amit Kumar Shah
Kai Huang
Pravan Omprakash
Yu Yun
item.description:
Authors: Xin Li, Guodong Ren, Haidong Lu, Kartik Samanta, Amit Kumar Shah, Kai Huang, Pravan Omprakash, Yu Yun, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 763-767
Abstract: Antiferroelectricity is a material property characterized by alternating electric dipoles spontaneously ordered in antiparallel directions. Antiferroelectrics are promising for energy storage, solid-state cooling, and memory technologies; however, these materials are scarce, and their scalability remains largely unexplored. In this work, we demonstrated that single-crystalline hafnia, a lead-free complementary metal-oxide semiconductor (CMOS)–compatible material, exhibits antiferroelectricity under compressive-strain conditions. We observed antiparallel sublattice polarization and stable double hysteresis in single-crystalline (111)-oriented epitaxial lanthanum (La)–doped hafnia films grown on yttrium-stabilized zirconia and showed that the antipolar orthorhombic phase of hafnia adheres to the Kittel model of antiferroelectricity. Compressive strain strengthens the orthorhombic order in thinner La-doped hafnia films, achieving a very high ordering temperature of 850°C in the two-dimensional limit, highlighting hafnia’s potential for advanced antiferroelectric devices.

item.title: Tracking danger on the peaks
item.dc:creator: Miriam Jackson
Amrit Thapa
item.description:
Authors: Miriam Jackson, Amrit Thapa
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 701-701
Abstract: The Earth is warming, but not all regions are warming equally. In high mountain areas, temperatures are generally increasing by 1.5 to 2 times the global average, sometimes with devastating consequences. A small or gradual change in the mountain cryosphere—perhaps progressive thawing of frozen ground or a flood from a small glacial lake—can suddenly turn into a cascade of catastrophes with enormous ramifications. Monitoring systems for the cryosphere in high mountain areas have traditionally been designed to look at individual components and changes. What are the temperature and depth of the permafrost, or how much area is covered by snow, and what is the related avalanche danger? Many of the monitoring and warning systems were designed for historical patterns of snowfall or rainfall, and a river gauge may no longer be adequate if there is greater flow in the rainy season, or increased sediment that could damage the gauge.

item.title: Direct monitoring of breaching in deltaic submarine landslides
item.dc:creator: Rebecca G. Englert
Matthieu J. B. Cartigny
Megan L. Baker
Sanem Acikalin
Dick Mastbergen
Niall Tracey
Sean C. Ruffell
Daniel H. Shugar
item.description:
Authors: Rebecca G. Englert, Matthieu J. B. Cartigny, Megan L. Baker, Sanem Acikalin, Dick Mastbergen, Niall Tracey, Sean C. Ruffell, Daniel H. Shugar, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 758-762
Abstract: Submarine landslides threaten seabed infrastructure and trigger the transport of globally important amounts of sediment, carbon, and pollutants to deep-sea environments. However, fully submarine landslides have never been directly monitored in nature. Past hypotheses for their failure mechanism and dynamics therefore remain unvalidated for natural settings, including that prolonged upslope-migrating failures (breaching) occur in sandy seafloor environments. In this work, we present direct underwater monitoring of fully submarine landslides at Homathko Delta in western Canada that retrogress slowly upslope, indicating breaching-type failure. Their prolonged rather than instantaneous nature has important implications for the stress that seabed structures must be designed to withstand. Prolonged landslides also initiate sustained sediment flows (turbidity currents) that efficiently transport sediment, carbon, and pollutants further offshore.

item.title: Giant elastoresistance in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene
item.dc:creator: Xuetao Ma
Zhaoyu Liu
Jiaqi Cai
Kenji Watanabe
Takashi Taniguchi
Xiaodong Xu
Jiun-Haw Chu
Matthew Yankowitz
item.description:
Authors: Xuetao Ma, Zhaoyu Liu, Jiaqi Cai, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Xiaodong Xu, Jiun-Haw Chu, Matthew Yankowitz
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 768-772
Abstract: Strongly correlated and topological phases in moiré materials are exquisitely sensitive to lattice geometry at both atomic and superlattice length scales. Twist angle, pressure, and strain directly modify the lattice and thus act as highly effective tuning parameters. Here, we examined electrical transport in twisted bilayer graphene subjected to continuous uniaxial strain. Near the magic angle (≈1.1°), devices exhibited a pronounced elastoresistance that depended on band filling and temperature, with a gauge factor more than two orders of magnitude larger than that of conventional metals. In selected doping regimes, the elastoresistance exhibited a Curie-Weiss–like temperature divergence. We discuss possible microscopic origins, including nematic fluctuations and enhanced electronic entropy from fluctuating isospin moments. Our work establishes uniaxial strain as a versatile probe of correlated physics in a moiré material.

item.title: A cellular atlas of the preinvasive breast cancer microenvironment
item.dc:creator: Siyuan He
Aatish Thennavan
Runmin Wei
Shanshan Bai
Jianzhuo Li
Chante Bethell
Emi Sei
Mitchell Rao
item.description:
Authors: Siyuan He, Aatish Thennavan, Runmin Wei, Shanshan Bai, Jianzhuo Li, Chante Bethell, Emi Sei, Mitchell Rao, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaef4622
Abstract: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common preinvasive breast cancer, however our knowledge of the DCIS tumor microenvironment (TME) remains limited. We constructed a comprehensive atlas of the TME in estrogen-receptor positive DCIS using fresh samples collected from normal breast tissues, DCIS and invasive breast cancers. We analyzed 854,911 cells from 159 patients by single cell RNA sequencing and 39 samples by spatial transcriptomics, which identified 9 cell types and 60 cell states. Our data shows remodeling of fibroblasts, vascular and basal cells that encircle the DCIS regions and immunosuppressive ducts that support the growth of the preinvasive cancer cells. This study delineates early alterations in the DCIS TME, including many changes that persist during invasive progression.

item.title: The cryosphere beyond a planetary safe operating space
item.dc:creator: Bo Su
Johan Rockström
Deliang Chen
Ingo Fetzer
Haipeng Feng
Gustaf Hugelius
Ricarda Winkelmann
Albert V. Norström
item.description:
Authors: Bo Su, Johan Rockström, Deliang Chen, Ingo Fetzer, Haipeng Feng, Gustaf Hugelius, Ricarda Winkelmann, Albert V. Norström, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaef5636
Abstract: The cryosphere plays a vital role in regulating planetary dynamics and habitability, yet it remains unclear whether its essential functions remain within a safe operating space (SOS) amid Anthropocene change. Here, we propose a cryosphere SOS and systematically evaluate its contributions to Earth system resilience using the planetary boundaries framework. Multiple lines of evidence indicate an accelerating and partly irreversible loss of cryospheric integrity, driven by amplifying feedbacks. Key cryospheric control variables either have left or are committed to departing from Holocene-like conditions. We conclude that the cryosphere has breached its SOS and is on a trajectory that locks in long-term risks for human societies and ecosystems. Safeguarding planetary resilience therefore requires explicit consideration of cryosphere change and its interactions across the Earth system.

item.title: Differentiation of stem-like CD4 <sup>+</sup> T cells modulates early effector responses in colorectal cancer
item.dc:creator: Yu Zhang
Hu Nie
Zixuan Dai
Liying Zhao
Yihong Wan
Yi Wang
Yikang Chen
Xinhua Chen
item.description:
Authors: Yu Zhang, Hu Nie, Zixuan Dai, Liying Zhao, Yihong Wan, Yi Wang, Yikang Chen, Xinhua Chen, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Article number: eady7788
Abstract: Strategies to improve cancer immunotherapy have largely focused on the intratumor immunosuppressive microenvironment, whereas approaches to amplify peripheral T cells and promote tumor recruitment have not been thoroughly explored. Using imaging mass cytometry in patients with colorectal cancer (CRC), we observed T helper 1 (T H 1)–like immune architectures in mismatch repair–deficient tumors associated with response to anti–programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) immunotherapy. By contrast, mismatch repair–proficient (pMMR) tumors showed regulatory T–dominant spatial interactions. Clonal analyses revealed that stem-like CD4 + T cells differentiated into T H 1-like cells after PD-1 blockade. In pMMR CRC mouse models, combined OX40 agonist and PD-1 blockade suppressed tumor progression by expanding Il7r + early effector CD4 + intermediates in tumor-draining lymph nodes, promoting migration and connection with T H 1-like cells. This was accompanied by interferon-γ–dependent induction of immunostimulatory monocyte-macrophages and CD8 + effector T cells. These findings suggest that leveraging peripheral CD4 + T cell amplification may improve immunotherapy responses.

item.title: Limited genomic predictability of complex trait evolution despite genotype-phenotype stability
item.dc:creator: J. A. Smiley-Rhodes
M. C. Bitter
S. Berardi
J. Beltz
D. A. Petrov
P. Schmidt
item.description:
Authors: J. A. Smiley-Rhodes, M. C. Bitter, S. Berardi, J. Beltz, D. A. Petrov, P. Schmidt
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Article number: eaee0342
Abstract: Whether genomic data can be used to effectively predict adaptation in natural populations is unknown. Here, we tested the efficacy of genomic prediction of complex trait evolution by monitoring genome-wide allele frequencies and pigmentation variation in genetically diverse populations of Drosophila melanogaster during evolution in both field mesocosms and a controlled, lab-based setting. At two points during trait evolution, we produced a high-powered, well-resolved genotype-phenotype map that exhibited marked stability across independent populations. Although we were able to use this map to correctly infer the direction of pigmentation evolution in both the lab and field settings, the particular loci responding to selection were largely unpredictable based on the direction of trait evolution itself. Our results hold implications for the promise, and limitations, of genomic prediction.

item.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak
item.dc:creator: Carla M. Bellomo
Sebastian D. Kehl
Daniel O. Alonso
Natalia Periolo
Andrea Gaweda
Santiago Vidal-Freire
Hade Ramos
Martín Lammel
item.description:
Authors: Carla M. Bellomo, Sebastian D. Kehl, Daniel O. Alonso, Natalia Periolo, Andrea Gaweda, Santiago Vidal-Freire, Hade Ramos, Martín Lammel, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaej1679
Abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.

item.title: Increased demographic turnover and isolation precede social fragmentation in Asian elephants
item.dc:creator: Anastasia E. Madsen
T. V. Pushpakumara
U. Sameera Weerathunga
Devaka K. Weerakoon
Shermin de Silva
item.description:
Authors: Anastasia E. Madsen, T. V. Pushpakumara, U. Sameera Weerathunga, Devaka K. Weerakoon, Shermin de Silva
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 792-798
Abstract: Humans and many other animals live in interconnected social communities that are essential for survival and well-being. In principle, communities can persist despite changes in constituent members. However, gradually accumulating changes to membership could push systems past critical thresholds into alternate states, restructuring patterns of connectivity. Such changes can further affect systemic resilience against disturbance. We investigated social network dynamics for 443 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years by tracking community membership and structure. Following accumulated demographic turnover, networks fractured into smaller and more isolated communities. Connections changed not only owing to loss of members but also modifications in relationships among remaining individuals. This provides empirical evidence of a persistent state change in the social network of a long-lived terrestrial mammal following gradually accumulating demographic turnover.

item.title: Carbon dioxide and amorphous water ices in the debris disk around β Pictoris
item.dc:creator: S. K. Betti
C. H. Chen
C. Xie
K. Worthen
S. Brittain
J. Najita
I. Rebollido
T. Beck
item.description:
Authors: S. K. Betti, C. H. Chen, C. Xie, K. Worthen, S. Brittain, J. Najita, I. Rebollido, T. Beck, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 742-745
Abstract: The star β Pictoris is orbited by a dusty debris disk, within which planet formation is occurring. The outer disk is sufficiently far from the star that volatile molecules are expected to freeze into solid ices. We observed the β Pictoris disk in the near-infrared using the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum shows features due to amorphous water ice (<7% crystallinity) and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) ice in both the 12 CO 2 and 13 CO 2 isotopologues. We infer that the CO 2 ice is intimately mixed with the water ice at a ratio of 1:10. This implies that the ices formed in cold conditions, likely in the interstellar medium. Frequent collisions within the debris disk are required to explain the observed uniform distribution of icy dust grains.

item.title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April–May 2026
item.dc:creator: Bas B. Oude Munnink
Samuel Cordey
Moussa Moïse Diagne
Jonathan Featherstone
Anabel Negredo
Sarah Temmam
Jenniffer Angulo
Carla M. Bellomo
item.description:
Authors: Bas B. Oude Munnink, Samuel Cordey, Moussa Moïse Diagne, Jonathan Featherstone, Anabel Negredo, Sarah Temmam, Jenniffer Angulo, Carla M. Bellomo, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaej1376
Abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.

item.title: The genetic landscape of canine tumors: Insights from the Canine Cancer Genome Atlas (CCGA)
item.dc:creator: Eugenio Mazzone
Laura Marconato
Antonella Fanelli
Luciano Cascione
Francesco Bertoni
Caterina Marchiò
Anna Sapino
Luca Aresu
item.description:
Authors: Eugenio Mazzone, Laura Marconato, Antonella Fanelli, Luciano Cascione, Francesco Bertoni, Caterina Marchiò, Anna Sapino, Luca Aresu
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Article number: eaeg8777
Abstract: The Canine Cancer Genome Atlas (CCGA, https://caninecancergenomeatlas.org/ ) is an open, accessible comparative oncology resource that harmonizes whole-exome data across 10 canine tumor histotypes. It aggregates 667 tumor-normal pairs with curated single-nucleotide variants, insertions and deletions, structural variants, and copy number aberrations. Cohort-depth stratification distinguished primary, exploratory, and descriptive analyses. Selection analyses identified 39 cancer drivers, including recurrent TP53 , PIK3CA , PTEN , SETD2 , MAP3K14 , and FAT4 alterations; copy number events included MYC amplifications and PTEN deletions. Direct comparison with matched human cancers revealed conserved and species-enriched oncogenic mechanisms, pathways, and therapeutic contexts. The CCGA standardizes alignment, variant calling, and annotation through consensus pipelines and provides downloadable data and interactive analyses. This reusable framework advances precision veterinary oncology and strengthens translational bridges to human cancer, supporting comparative and translational research.

item.title: TMEM184 proteins are Ca <sup>2+</sup> uptake transporters in lysosomes
item.dc:creator: Weijie Cai
Yalan Wang
Fangqian Huang
Yulou Zhang
Mingxue Gu
Chuanyan Yang
Ping Li
Wenfeng Jiang
item.description:
Authors: Weijie Cai, Yalan Wang, Fangqian Huang, Yulou Zhang, Mingxue Gu, Chuanyan Yang, Ping Li, Wenfeng Jiang, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Article number: eaeh3996
Abstract: Lysosomal Ca 2+ release from acidic stores is critical for lysosomal function, yet the molecular identity of the Ca 2+ uptake conduit has remained elusive. We used a Ca 2+ -imaging–based genetic screen of the lysosomal membrane proteome to identify TMEM184 family proteins as lysosomal Ca 2+ transporters (LyCaTs) essential for Ca 2+ uptake and refilling. TMEM184 selectively transported Ca 2+ while excluding monovalent cations. Loss of TMEM184B/C depleted lysosomal Ca 2+ stores, diminished Ca 2+ release, and disrupted lysosomal exocytosis, biogenesis, and membrane repair, thus phenocopying the release channel transient receptor potential mucolipin 1 (TRPML1) deficiency. Moreover, a human TMEM184B mutation associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder compromised lysosomal Ca 2+ transport, and Tmem184b -deficient mice exhibited profound motor impairment. Thus, TMEM184 constitutes the long-sought Ca 2+ uptake and refilling mechanism that governs lysosomal signaling and homeostasis.

item.title: Quantitative measurement of viscosity in two-dimensional electron fluids
item.dc:creator: Yihang Zeng
Haoyu Guo
Olivia M. Ghosh
Kenji Watanabe
Takashi Taniguchi
Leonid S. Levitov
Cory R. Dean
item.description:
Authors: Yihang Zeng, Haoyu Guo, Olivia M. Ghosh, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Leonid S. Levitov, Cory R. Dean
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 786-791
Abstract: Electron hydrodynamics is an emerging framework that describes dynamics of interacting electron systems as conventional fluids. Although evidence for hydrodynamic-like transport has been reported in a variety of two-dimensional materials, precise quantitative measurement of the core parameter, electron viscosity, remains challenging. In this work, we demonstrate that magnetoresistance in Corbino-shaped graphene devices offers a simultaneous ohmmeter and viscosometer capability, allowing us to disentangle the individual ohmic and viscous contributions to transport, even near viscous-ohmic crossover. In both monolayer and bilayer graphene, the effective electron-electron scattering rate scales linearly with temperature, deviating markedly from the T 2 dependence expected in conventional Fermi liquids. Instead, it is consistent with a recently identified tomographic fluid regime, theoretically predicted to be generic for two-dimensional electron systems.

item.title: A trapped catalytic product acts as molecular glue for innate immune signalosome assembly
item.dc:creator: Qi Liu
Zhongjian Bai
Tianyi Liu
Fangshuai Jia
Yi Ji
Canxi Chen
Yao Gong
Liuyuan Duan
item.description:
Authors: Qi Liu, Zhongjian Bai, Tianyi Liu, Fangshuai Jia, Yi Ji, Canxi Chen, Yao Gong, Liuyuan Duan, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Article number: eaef3150
Abstract: Innate immune systems of living organisms are essential for host defense. Central to these systems is the Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain, an evolutionarily conserved module. From antiphage systems in prokaryotes to innate immune systems in plants, TIR domains have catalytic activity. However, TIR domains within animal innate immune receptors, such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs), have been considered as scaffolds for adaptor recruitment. We report that the TLR4 TIR domain possesses an allosterically activated nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) hydrolase (NADase) activity that operates in a single-turnover manner. Its product, adenosine diphosphate ribose, is not released but entrapped as a “molecular glue,” stabilizing a composite catalytic pocket with adaptor TIR domain–containing adaptor protein (TIRAP) to nucleate signalosome assembly. This “produce-and-trap” mechanism represents a signaling mode that integrates enzymatic activity with adaptor function to drive downstream signaling.

item.title: Poisoned hunting weapons, megafauna, and plant use at a 125,000-year-old Arabian paleolakeshore
item.dc:creator: Chris Clarkson
Gilbert J. Price
Amir Kalifi
Giacomo Losi
Carney Matheson
Faisal Al-Jibreen
Abdullah M. Alsharekh
Simon J. Armitage
item.description:
Authors: Chris Clarkson, Gilbert J. Price, Amir Kalifi, Giacomo Losi, Carney Matheson, Faisal Al-Jibreen, Abdullah M. Alsharekh, Simon J. Armitage, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 746-751
Abstract: After the African origin of Homo sapiens , multiple dispersals radiated into Asia, yet the Saharo-Arabian archaeological record remains sparse. In this study, we report on ‘Uruq Aljelibah, a Middle Paleolithic site dated to ~125,000 years ago (marine isotope stage 5e) and located on the shore of Mundafan paleolake, Saudi Arabia. Levallois assemblages, refits, and megafaunal associations indicate in situ tool production and carcass processing. Stone tool residues, use-wear, and biomarkers reveal animal and plant processing, including palms, tubers, trees, and shrubs. Several points exhibit impact damage and poison residues (from Acokanthera schimperi ), indicating use as hafted weapon tips within composite hunting systems. Megafaunal remains include hippopotamus, buffalo, gazelle, ostrich, and camel, illuminating hominin use of freshwater and grassland ecosystems.

item.title: Climate aridity amplifies global riverine nitrate beyond human inputs
item.dc:creator: Kayalvizhi Sadayappan
Li Li
item.description:
Authors: Kayalvizhi Sadayappan, Li Li
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 773-778
Abstract: Nitrate pollution is widely perceived as a signature of human inputs. Here we show, with machine-learning reconstructed global maps, that climate aridity is also a dominant driver, systematically elevating nitrate concentrations across land-use gradients and creating unexpected hotspots beyond major agricultural and urban centers. Across ~2.9 million river segments worldwide, nitrate concentrations exceed ecological and health thresholds across ~33 and 2% of global land area, affecting ~5.6 billion (73%) and 0.5 billion (6%) people, respectively. Ecological threshold exceedance occurs mostly in headwaters, and about half of the health threshold exceedance occurs in middle-income countries and sparsely populated landscapes. These findings cast nitrate pollution as an aridity-amplified risk, suggesting that aridification may increase nitrate exposure even without additional human inputs. They call for regulatory standards that reflect risks across broad concentration ranges.

item.title: Atmospheric O <sub>2</sub> reveals a strengthening ocean carbon sink and a stagnant net land sink since 1990
item.dc:creator: Eric J. Morgan
Yuming Jin
Elena Kozlova
Andrew J. Watson
Andrew C. Manning
Sönke Zaehle
Yasunori Tohjima
Xin Lan
item.description:
Authors: Eric J. Morgan, Yuming Jin, Elena Kozlova, Andrew J. Watson, Andrew C. Manning, Sönke Zaehle, Yasunori Tohjima, Xin Lan, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 799-803
Abstract: The global ocean and land biosphere absorb roughly half of fossil fuel carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions. The temporal evolution of these sinks remains difficult to quantify owing to data sparsity. Leveraging 30+ years of atmospheric oxygen (O 2 ) and CO 2 observations, we find that the ocean carbon sink increased by 0.63 ± 0.19 petagrams of carbon per year per decade (Pg C year −1 decade −1 ) (a mean of 2.8 ± 0.4 Pg C year −1 ), accounting for 35% of fossil emissions between 1990 and 2019. The net land sink shows no robust trend (with a mean of 1.0 ± 0.5 Pg C year −1 , accounting for 13% of fossil emissions), despite large decadal variability. These results challenge many process-based model simulations of the land and ocean sinks, questioning their ability to accurately predict future climate states.

item.title: ESCRT-0 condensation and cargo clustering drive extracellular vesicle budding from cilia
item.dc:creator: Mingli Zhu
Yash Raj
Gary A. Bradshaw
Henry T. Phan
Catalina Kretschmar
Marian Kalocsay
Maxence V. Nachury
item.description:
Authors: Mingli Zhu, Yash Raj, Gary A. Bradshaw, Henry T. Phan, Catalina Kretschmar, Marian Kalocsay, Maxence V. Nachury
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Article number: eaej7530
Abstract: Cilia-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) mediate cell-cell communication and remove signaling molecules from cilia. The Hedgehog receptor Smoothened (SMO) is selected for packaging into ciliary EVs by ubiquitin chains, but how cargo selection is coupled to EV budding remains unknown. In this work, working in mouse kidney cells, we found that the ubiquitin reader endosomal sorting complex required for transport–0 (ESCRT-0) orchestrates both cargo selection and EV biogenesis. Unlike the conventional ESCRT pathway, SMO secretion did not require the ESCRT-III membrane scission machinery. Instead, ESCRT-0 condensed at the ciliary tip, where it clustered ubiquitinated SMO to drive EV biogenesis. Disrupting ESCRT-0 condensation blocked SMO secretion, and combining forced recruitment of ESCRT-0 with optogenetic clustering of SMO was sufficient to reconstitute EV budding. Thus, ESCRT-0 condensation and cargo clustering constitute a minimal module for ESCRT-III–independent reverse-topology budding.

item.title: Early epidemiological and spatial assessment of the Bundibugyo virus outbreak 2026
item.dc:creator: Dav M. Ebengo
Pierre Akilimali
Tania Bishola Tshitenge
Ciara Judge
Bernardo Gutierrez

item.description:
Authors: Dav M. Ebengo, Pierre Akilimali, Tania Bishola Tshitenge, Ciara Judge, Bernardo Gutierrez, Ellie Bourgikos, Olivier le Polain de Waroux, Eddy Kinganda-Lusamaki, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaej4586
Abstract: A Bundibugyo virus outbreak was first reported on May 15th, 2026 in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with multiple cases reported across health zones during the early phase of the outbreak and suggestions of circulation weeks prior to detection. We pair highly resolved case and testing records with human mobility data to investigate the early outbreak dynamics of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD). We show that human movement was a principle driver of early spatial expansion between May 10th and June 1st when the number of health zones and health areas reporting positive cases increased by 12 and 49, respectively. The early doubling time was estimated at ~10 days. Our work shows the rapid spatial expansion and growth of BVD with implications for intervention strategies.

item.title: Geodetic observations in West Antarctica reveal geodynamically consistent 3D mantle viscosity
item.dc:creator: Donna L. dePolo
Tao Yuan
Matt A. King
Shijie Zhong
item.description:
Authors: Donna L. dePolo, Tao Yuan, Matt A. King, Shijie Zhong
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6825; Pages: 752-757
Abstract: The rapid ice loss in West Antarctica since the 1990s has led to substantial ice surface lowering, regional bedrock uplift, and gravity reduction, as measured by geodetic observations. The bedrock (crustal) motions and gravity changes result from glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA), a process controlled by Earth’s viscoelastic properties and deglaciation history. In this study, we present GIA models with geodynamically consistent three-dimensional mantle viscoelastic structures and reconstructed ice history for Antarctica from 1900 to 2020, which explain both the observed Global Navigation Satellite System crustal motions and Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment gravity changes in West Antarctica. This study demonstrates that a mantle rheology including a weak asthenosphere and temperature-dependent viscosity is consistent with both mantle convection at million-year timescales and ongoing decadal GIA occurring in West Antarctica.

item.title: Melting and resistivity of iron at Earth core conditions using pulsed Joule heating
item.dc:creator: Zachary M. Geballe
Jing Yang
Vasilije V. Dobrosavljevic
Francesca Miozzi
Nathan Sime
Suzy M. Vitale
Peter E. Driscoll

item.description:
Authors: Zachary M. Geballe, Jing Yang, Vasilije V. Dobrosavljevic, Francesca Miozzi, Nathan Sime, Suzy M. Vitale, Peter E. Driscoll, Peter E. van Keken, et al.
Journal: Science; Article number: eaeh5267
Abstract: The melting temperature and electrical resistivity of iron at high pressure are essential for understanding Earth’s core. Here we use a new high-pressure method – microsecond pulsed Joule heating in diamond anvil cells – to identify melting and measure resistivity of solid and liquid iron. More than 300 reproducible melting measurements indicate a surprisingly shallow melting curve, reaching 6 K/GPa and 4160 ± 80 K at 200 GPa. Extrapolating in pressure and iron alloy composition, and combining with our 76 μ Ω cm measurement of liquid iron’s resistivity, we infer a relatively cold core-mantle boundary (3430 K) with a low adiabatic outer core heat flow (9.8 TW). This suggests thermal convection alone could have powered the geodynamo prior to inner core formation and that today’s lowermost mantle is fully solid.

item.title: Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
item.dc:creator: Yvette Running Horse Collin
item.description:
Authors: Yvette Running Horse Collin
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 575-575
Abstract: As the use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) increases, alarms are being raised about how the technology could replace human contribution, override human supervision, ignore ethical and technical guardrails, and cause increasingly irreparable harm to the environment. This creates potentially destructive outcomes for life on Earth. From a traditional Indigenous science perspective, such possibilities in themselves would be enough to immediately stop presently configured AI releases. In a Lakota context, science must ensure as little harm as possible is done to life. Therefore, AI as presently configured simply would not qualify to advance further from an ethical and scientific standpoint. Indigenous science asks something fundamentally different than what AI presently seeks to, or can, answer. But that does not mean that future forms of AI can never align with Indigenous science.

item.title: Tumor metastasis co-opts liver hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression
item.dc:creator: Qiang Pan
Xuege Wang
Yaqi Li
Ni Li
Ying Han
Guoying Zhang
Jiacheng Guo
Le Zhang
item.description:
Authors: Qiang Pan, Xuege Wang, Yaqi Li, Ni Li, Ying Han, Guoying Zhang, Jiacheng Guo, Le Zhang, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Article number: eaea3046
Abstract: Cancer-associated hematopoietic abnormalities contribute to systemic immunosuppression. However, whether tumors can initiate localized extramedullary hematopoiesis to suppress antitumor immunity remains unclear. In this study, we identify a distinct form of hepatic hematopoiesis driven by liver metastasis–associated hematopoietic stem cells (LM-HSCs). Liver metastases establish ectopic periportal hematopoietic niches that recruit bone marrow HSCs through Kupffer cell–dependent C-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CCR1) signaling. Although LM-HSCs retain self-renewal and multipotency, cAMP response element–binding protein (CREB) activation skews their differentiation toward the myeloid lineage, particularly annexin A1–positive (ANXA1 + ) immature neutrophils. These neutrophils produce glucocorticoids, which activate glucocorticoid receptor signaling in a paracrine manner and induce immune checkpoint receptor expression and functional anergy in CD8 + T and natural killer cells. Collectively, these findings suggest that liver metastases reprograms hepatic hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression.

item.title: Discovering molecular modulators with nanoswitch screening
item.dc:creator: Clinton H. Hansen
Mark Lipstein
Sarah C. Erlandson
Tobias Schwalbe
Sylvie G. Bernier
Peter Gmeiner
Andrew C. Kruse
Wesley P. Wong
item.description:
Authors: Clinton H. Hansen, Mark Lipstein, Sarah C. Erlandson, Tobias Schwalbe, Sylvie G. Bernier, Peter Gmeiner, Andrew C. Kruse, Wesley P. Wong
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Article number: eadt7185
Abstract: Molecules that modulate protein-protein interactions, including through ternary complex formation, have been established as key therapeutics. Yet they can be challenging to discover, as standard screening approaches often lack throughput or fail to directly assay multibody interactions. We addressed this by combining DNA nanoswitch–based selection of nucleotide-encoded libraries with next-generation sequencing to create FIND (Functional Interaction–based Nanoswitch Discovery), which enables ultrahigh-throughput discovery of compounds that induce or increase protein-protein interactions. We demonstrate FIND by discovering nanobodies that stabilize the interaction between angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 and the receptor-binding domain of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 and by discovering agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor gamma from a DNA-barcoded small-molecule library. By enabling rapid discovery of molecular modulators, FIND could lead to new therapeutics across many conditions.

item.title: Quantum gas microscopy of three-flavor Hubbard systems
item.dc:creator: Jirayu Mongkolkiattichai
Liyu Liu
Sohail Dasgupta
Kaden R. A. Hazzard
Peter Schauss
item.description:
Authors: Jirayu Mongkolkiattichai, Liyu Liu, Sohail Dasgupta, Kaden R. A. Hazzard, Peter Schauss
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 665-669
Abstract: Hubbard systems are paradigmatic realizations of strongly correlated many-body systems. Introducing additional species breaks the SU(2) symmetry of the Hubbard model and leads to a wide variety of new exotic quantum phases. Here, we extended quantum gas microscopy to three-flavor Fermi lattice gases in the Hubbard regime. Relying on site- and flavor-resolved detection, we studied the phase diagram of the three-flavor Hubbard model and found signatures of flavor-selective localization and selective pairing at temperatures down to the tunneling energy scale. Our measurements were then compared with numerical linked-cluster expansion calculations. Further increase of phase space density may enable the observation of a distinct pair Mott phase at half filling and shows a path toward the study of color superfluidity and other aspects of quantum chromodynamics.

item.title: Targeting hormone conversion through dietary fiber improves polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome
item.dc:creator: Xinyu Qi
Hong Chen
Qixing Nie
Hongyu Niu
Yong Ding
Xi Luo
Manfei Si
Shuqi Wu
item.description:
Authors: Xinyu Qi, Hong Chen, Qixing Nie, Hongyu Niu, Yong Ding, Xi Luo, Manfei Si, Shuqi Wu, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Article number: eaed8952
Abstract: Excessive androgens serve as a primary driver for many phenotypic features of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). Although dietary fiber has been shown to alleviate PMOS, its effects on androgen concentrations and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In a clinical trial, we demonstrated that a dietary fiber combination consisting of inulin, resistant starch, and β-glucan reduces androgen concentrations in patients’ plasma. Mechanistically, dietary fiber increased the abundance of Bacteroides xylanisolven s, which converts androstenedione into a nonandrogenic secondary hormone metabolite we named coproandrosterone, which is further metabolized by gut microbiota into dihydro-coproandrosterone. This metabolic pathway was validated in a mouse model. These findings highlight the potential of dietary fiber to alleviate PMOS by modulating androgen homeostasis through gut microbiota, offering insights for prebiotic and probiotic therapies.

item.dc:creator: Gino Caspari

Authors: Gino Caspari, Timur Sadykov, Daria Fomicheva, Jegor Blochin, Dominic Armbruster, Oliver Happel, Natalia Ryabogina, Kseniia Boxleitner, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 649-653
Abstract: Cannabis is the world’s most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. We show that the practice of cannabis consumption dates back at least 2800 years, anchoring debates around contemporary usage and informing discussions on cannabis in medicine, public health, law, and industry.

item.title: Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition
item.dc:creator: Stina Börchers
Giulia Mazzini
Henrik Zetterberg
Christoffer Clemmensen
item.description:
Authors: Stina Börchers, Giulia Mazzini, Henrik Zetterberg, Christoffer Clemmensen
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 633-640
Abstract: Pharmacotherapies for obesity and type 2 diabetes are increasingly being evaluated for their effects on cognition and brain health. Evidence from preclinical models, observational cohorts, and clinical trials has intensified interest, but findings remain mixed. A central challenge is to determine whether potential cognitive effects arise from direct actions on neural circuits, indirect consequences of improved cardiometabolic health, or both. This Review examines the evidence across cardiometabolic disease, aging, and Alzheimer’s disease, focusing on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)–based therapies and combination approaches that engage glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon, and amylin pathways. We assess how receptor pharmacology, brain exposure, metabolic context, and disease stage shape cognitive outcomes and discuss how mechanistic clarity could guide therapies aimed at preserving or improving cognition.

Abstract: Ultracold atom platforms enable low temperatures and long free evolution times, which are crucial for fundamental physics tests and atom interferometry. The lowest equivalent temperature reported in such a system is 38 pK with a free expansion time of 2 s, achieved in atom-chip-based magnetic traps in microgravity. Optical dipole trap (ODT) systems offer better optical access and the flexibility to condense both magnetic and non-magnetic atoms, but have not been used to prepare quantum degenerate gases under microgravity conditions. Here we report an ODT-based Bose-Einstein condensate created aboard the China Space Station, containing 2.0 × 10 4 atoms, reaching an equivalent temperature of 9.7 − 2.7 + 3.2 pK with a free expansion time of 7.0 s. This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space.

item.dc:creator: Hadas Raviv
Arkadii Tsyhanov
Kira Gousios

item.description:
Authors: Hadas Raviv, Arkadii Tsyhanov, Kira Gousios, Aja Altenhof, Haocheng Wang, Berlin Chen, Ofri Raviv, Tal Rosenwein, et al.

Abstract: Children learn to understand and speak from the speech around them, yet how that everyday input shapes learning remains unresolved. Large language models show that language is learnable from data, but their scale and training conditions differ sharply from a child’s natural experience. We trained cognitively feasible, child-specific models on longitudinal home recordings from eight children across their first 1000 days of life. Each model learned incrementally from a single child’s ordered speech input without prior linguistic knowledge, developing phoneme-like and word-form representations that tracked each child’s learning pace. Learning was dependent on dense daily sampling and replay of recent input, indicating that both experience- and memory-related processes are necessary. These findings show that everyday experience contains sufficient structure for language learning and establish child-specific modeling for testing developmental theories.

item.dc:creator: Jiasen Niu
Maialen Ortego Larrazabal
Thomas Gozlinski
Yudai Sato
Koen M. Bastiaans
Tjerk Benschop

Authors: Jiasen Niu, Maialen Ortego Larrazabal, Thomas Gozlinski, Yudai Sato, Koen M. Bastiaans, Tjerk Benschop, Jian-Feng Ge, Yaroslav M. Blanter, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 682-685
Abstract: The pseudogap stands out in the phase diagram of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors because its origin and relationship to superconductivity remain elusive. The origin of the pseudogap has been debated, with competing hypotheses attributing it to preformed electron pairs or local order, such as charge density waves. We present unambiguous evidence supporting the pairing scenario, using local shot-noise spectroscopy measurements in Bi 2 Sr 2 CaCu 2 O 8+δ . Our data demonstrate that the pseudogap energy coincides with the onset of electron pairing and is spatially heterogeneous with values reaching up to 70 milli–electron volts. Our results exclude a pure local order origin of the pseudogap, link the pseudogap to Cooper pair formation, and suggest that the limiting factor for higher critical temperature in cuprates is phase coherence.

Abstract: The 2020 United States Census adopted differential privacy to protect individual confidentiality, adding calibrated noise to summary demographic measurements that are then reconciled into population tables. We developed BlueDown, a postprocessing algorithm that combines techniques from linear regression and constrained optimization while exploiting measurement structure for efficiency. On 2020 Census data, BlueDown reduced the error of groupings by race at the county level by 21 to 36% and of all county-level groupings by 9 to 58%; at the tract level, it reduced error of groupings by housing type by 38 to 61%. These gains came at no cost to confidentiality or computational efficiency and would improve the validity of research relying on this definitive dataset and analyses used to guide the distribution of more than $1.5 trillion in annual federal spending.

item.dc:creator: Changfeng Su

item.description:
Authors: Changfeng Su, Yang Li, Zhongzheng Deng, Shiyu Zhong, Jiyuan Hu, Xueshi Li, Qiao Li, Qingping Sun
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 670-675
Abstract: Elastocaloric cooling (eC) uses shape memory alloys (SMAs) as energy-efficient, eco-friendly refrigerants. However, cost-effectively fabricating SMAs into fatigue-resistant, heat transfer–enhanced structures remains a key obstacle to commercialization of the eC technology. We introduce a “stamping and stacking” (S-S) method for producing porous, fatigue-resistant SMA structures. Honeycomb-like chips are stamped from nitinol (NiTi) thin sheets and then stacked into a layered tubular structure to increase heat exchange surface and at the same time avoid buckling and splitting failures encountered in existing SMA structures. The stacked structure endures >10 8 compression cycles and can deliver high specific cooling power of 3850 watts per kilogram. Our S-S method reduces fabrication costs by one order of magnitude compared with existing approaches, enabling mass production of eC refrigerant structures for commercial deployment.

item.title: Echoes of the Anthropocene: Noise pollution as a global threat
item.dc:creator: Hansjoerg P. Kunc
Rouven Schmidt
item.description:
Authors: Hansjoerg P. Kunc, Rouven Schmidt
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 660-664
Abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a rapidly expanding global pollutant, but its effects across biological levels from individuals to ecosystems remain unquantified. We conducted phylogenetically controlled meta-analyses of 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species with ranges that span six continents. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental, or behavioral trait in 80% of species studied, with declines in fitness and abundance and disruptions of predator-prey interactions. Effects occurred in every habitat, although response mechanisms varied for some traits and species, creating winners and losers. Only multispecies analyses can reveal such species- and ecosystem-level impacts of anthropogenic stressors. Our results establish noise as a novel selection pressure reshaping ecosystem dynamics and as a pervasive stressor requiring soundscape protection alongside habitat conservation.

item.description:
Authors: Fumiaki Tomita, Tianhaozhe Sun, Motoyuki Kido, Takeshi Iinuma, Naoki Uchida, Yusaku Ohta, Ryota Hino, Jiangheng He, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 676-681
Abstract: How and when the subduction megathrust recovers its locking state after a great earthquake is important to understanding earthquake-cycle physics and future hazards. Here we report the delineation of the relocking process after the 2011 magnitude 9 Tohoku earthquake with 14 years of postseismic seafloor geodetic observations. These data, combined with onshore geodetic observations, analyses of repeating earthquakes, and numerical modeling, reveal how the recovery of locking is interrupted by afterslip on the megathrust and accompanied by stress relaxation in the viscoelastic upper mantle. The results indicate that the megathrust has already arrived at a locking state today similar to that before the earthquake despite the ongoing stress relaxation. The acquired knowledge aids understanding of megathrust earthquake cycles at other subduction zones.

item.title: Obesity management medications: The way forward
item.dc:creator: Matthias Blüher
item.description:
Authors: Matthias Blüher
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 626-632
Abstract: Obesity is now widely recognized as a chronic progressive condition. The altered biological mechanisms that cause obesity frequently require long-term treatment, including pharmacotherapies or bariatric surgery. In recent decades, the pathophysiology of obesity has been understood to an extent that obesity management medication (OMM) discovery could be rationally pursued. Advances in defining the regulation of food intake and energy expenditure by molecular communication from peripheral organs to the brain led to the development of OMMs that appear capable of safely achieving scalable and sustained body weight loss. However, side effects, heterogeneous treatment responses, long-term metabolic adaptations, adherence, and other factors may limit the use of existing OMMs and justify the development of additional medications to improve the health of people living with obesity.

item.title: Glacial abrupt transitions in ocean circulation were much slower than ice-core records imply
item.dc:creator: Xiyu Dong
Xu Zhang
Yuchen Sun
Gayatri Kathayat
Youwei Li
Sune O. Rasmussen
Anders Svensson
Christo Buizert
item.description:
Authors: Xiyu Dong, Xu Zhang, Yuchen Sun, Gayatri Kathayat, Youwei Li, Sune O. Rasmussen, Anders Svensson, Christo Buizert, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 654-659
Abstract: Dansgaard-Oeschger (DO) events during the last ice age are thought to reflect rapid shifts in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Greenland ice cores suggest warming transitions within only a few decades—or even just over 10 years. Using precisely dated speleothem oxygen-isotope records from the Asian monsoon region, we have shown that the same DO warmings unfolded over more than a century. Isotope modeling revealed that Greenland records primarily capture a rapid atmospheric reorganization triggered by the initial sea-ice retreat in the northeastern North Atlantic, whereas the parallel AMOC recovery and hemispheric thermal adjustment proceeded much more slowly. These findings reveal that natural AMOC transitions evolved more slowly than the rapid North Greenland oxygen-isotope shifts would imply, thereby refining our understanding of “abruptness” during DO events.

item.title: When fat adapts: From physiological remodeling to disease
item.dc:creator: Karima Drareni
Patrick Seale
item.description:
Authors: Karima Drareni, Patrick Seale
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6824; Pages: 618-625
Abstract: Adipose tissue undergoes extensive remodeling to adapt to changing physiological demands. This plasticity encompasses changes in adipocyte metabolism and number, extracellular matrix organization, vascularization, immune composition, and innervation. When coordinated, these processes preserve energy buffering, thermogenesis, endocrine function, and local tissue support. Pathological adipose tissue remodeling drives obesity-related complications and contributes to many diseases involving organ-associated adipose depots throughout the body. In cancer, tumor-associated fat can develop a metabolic and fibroinflammatory niche that promotes tumor growth and invasion, and remodeling of other depots can directly disrupt neighboring tissues. Recent studies have identified mesenchymal, immune, vascular, and adipocyte states that govern adaptive or pathological outcomes. These findings broaden therapeutic goals beyond reducing fat mass toward restoring adipogenesis, substrate turnover, thermogenic capacity, and tissue-niche function.

item.title: The global geography of threats to freshwater biodiversity
item.dc:creator: Christophe Brabant
Laura Pollock
Jonas Geldmann
Mette Bendixen
Lise Comte
Harith Farooq
Katherine Hébert
Bernhard Lehner
item.description:
Authors: Christophe Brabant, Laura Pollock, Jonas Geldmann, Mette Bendixen, Lise Comte, Harith Farooq, Katherine Hébert, Bernhard Lehner, et al.
Journal: Science; Volume: 394; Issue: 6823; Pages: 510-514
Abstract: Human activities are eroding biodiversity, especially in freshwater systems. Despite major advances in quantifying species vulnerability and threats, we still lack a crucial understanding of where threats are affecting freshwater species globally. Here, we produced a species-centered spatial assessment of threats, mapping the impact of 45 threats across 21,490 freshwater species of amphibians, fish, mammals, odonates, and reptiles. We found that species in highly developed and water-managed regions are strongly affected by multiple overlapping threats. Although threats vary across taxa and regions, increasing threat probabilities elevate extinction risk and population declines, with freshwater species experiencing greater threat intensity and distinct spatial patterns than terrestrial species. Our findings establish a spatially explicit baseline for targeting the most urgently needed freshwater conservation and management interventions.
